lines: Morgan Kim
+1 (555) 010-8173 | morgan.kim@example.com | example.com/code/mkim
EDUCATION
Clearwater Institute of Technology | B.S. in Electrical Engineering | Metro City, USA | Sep 2017 - May 2021
EXPERIENCE
Voltline Robotics | Embedded Software Engineer | Metro City, USA | Mar 2023 - Jun 2025
- Improved update speed by 60% by compressing firmware images and resuming interrupted downloads.
- Wrote a hardware-in-the-loop test rig that ran 400 motor-control tests on every firmware build.
- Added a crash logger that saved the last 2 seconds of sensor data to flash, which found the root cause of 5 field failures.
- Sampled the motor's 5 kHz vibration signal at 8 kHz so the fault detector could capture it without aliasing.
- Fixed a race condition on the counter shared by the interrupt handler and the main loop by declaring the counter volatile.
- Rewrote the motor-controller firmware for a warehouse robot fleet of 300 units, cutting control-loop jitter from 120 to 15 microseconds and field motor faults by 60%.
Clearwater Sensors | Hardware Test Engineer | Metro City, USA | Apr 2022 - Feb 2023
- Automated end-of-line tests for a humidity sensor, cutting test time per unit from 90 to 25 seconds across 20,000 units a month.
- Traced a batch of early field failures to a solder-paste change; the findings updated the reflow profile and cut returns from 2.1% to 0.4%.
- Wrote the calibration procedure for the sensor line, cutting calibration drift complaints from 15 to 2 a quarter.
- Designed a test fixture that checked 8 boards at once, raising station throughput from 40 to 150 boards an hour.
PROJECTS
Low-Power Weather Station | Independent Project | C, STM32 | Jan 2025 - Present
- Engineered a next-generation, innovation-driven IoT solution that redefines sustainable environmental sensing.
- Cut average current from 4.2 mA to 0.9 mA by sleeping between readings and batching radio transmissions.
- Published the schematics and firmware openly, and a local school built two stations from them.
Formula Student Electric Car | Electronics Lead, Team of 12 | C | Sep 2019 - May 2021
- Worked on firmware and testing for the robot fleet's motor controllers.
- The CAN-bus firmware for the dashboard was written and tested against the motor controller before each race.
- Rewrote motor-control firmware for a fleet of about 300 robots, cutting control-loop jitter eightfold and motor faults by more than half.
SKILLS
Tools: C, C++, STM32, oscilloscopes, FPGA
Methods: firmware, hardware-in-the-loop testing, CAN, low-power design

items.says: The code URL does not clearly identify itself as a GitHub or portfolio link.
items.because: Readers should be able to recognize what it links to.

items.says: Add LinkedIn if you use it professionally.
Consider adding a city.
items.because: It can help recruiters understand your location.

items.says: Consider moving Education below Experience and Projects.
items.because: Your post-graduation experience is substantial enough to lead.

items.says: Clarify what “update speed” measures and how the 60% improvement was measured.
items.because: Readers need to know what improved.

items.says: Add the outcome enabled by the test rig if you can substantiate it.
items.because: Defect detection, coverage, or time saved would show its impact.

items.says: Clarify whether the logger captured data before a crash or fault and how it isolated the failures.
Sampling a 5 kHz signal at 8 kHz cannot capture it without aliasing.
items.because: The sampling rate must exceed twice the highest frequency of interest, with appropriate anti-alias filtering.

items.says: Declaring a shared counter volatile is not, by itself, a reliable race-condition fix.
items.because: Volatile does not generally make shared access atomic or provide synchronization.

items.says: Move the motor-controller rewrite earlier in the role.
items.because: It is the strongest Voltline bullet.

items.says: Make the measurement period and the link between the firmware change and fewer motor faults defensible.
Clarify that the monthly volume refers to the affected line or process.
items.because: It does not necessarily represent units you personally tested.

items.says: Be prepared to explain how the solder-paste change and reflow-profile update were verified.
Specify the period covered by the complaints comparison if you can.
items.because: It will help readers judge the improvement.

items.says: Be ready to explain how you measured station throughput.
Remove the promotional “next-generation, innovation-driven” line.
items.because: It gives no evidence of what you built or why it is technically notable.

items.says: Make the public schematics and firmware accessible through the header or a project link.
Show what you led and how you worked with the team, if you can support it.
items.because: The bullets do not yet substantiate the Electronics Lead title.

items.says: The robot-fleet bullet appears misattributed to the Formula Student electric car project.
items.because: It is inconsistent with the car team and conflicts with the Voltline robot-fleet material.

items.says: Clarify your contribution and what the CAN-bus testing established.
items.because: The bullet is vague and passive.

items.says: The robot-fleet accomplishment appears duplicated and misattributed.
items.because: It closely repeats Voltline’s fleet size and results and is difficult to reconcile with the Formula Student project.

items.says: Separate the listed skills into accurate categories.
items.because: The Tools category mixes languages, a microcontroller platform, test equipment, and FPGA experience.

items.says: Include FPGA only if you can discuss hands-on experience with it.
Organize these skills by type.
items.because: The Methods category mixes a work area, test approach, communications bus, and design concern.

items.says: Consider adding specific technologies demonstrated in your experience if you can discuss them in an interview.
Put the most role-relevant skills first.
